title: Machine learning fundamentals
text: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which models learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. Supervised learning uses labeled examples, while unsupervised learning discovers structure such as clusters in unlabeled data.

title: Neural networks and layers
text: A neural network stacks layers of artificial neurons. Each layer applies a linear transformation followed by a nonlinear activation, and training adjusts the weights with gradient descent to minimize a loss function.

title: Transformer architecture
text: The transformer architecture relies on self-attention so every token can attend to every other token in a sequence. Transformers power modern large language models and sentence embedding models alike.

title: Sentence embedding models
text: Sentence embedding models map text into fixed-size vectors so that semantically similar sentences land close together in the vector space. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a popular distilled sentence transformer that produces 384-dimensional embeddings.

title: Model quantization basics
text: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights, for example from 32-bit floating point to 8-bit integers. INT8 quantization shrinks model files dramatically and speeds up inference at the cost of a small accuracy drop.

title: Knowledge distillation
text: Knowledge distillation trains a small student model to imitate a larger teacher model. Distilled models keep much of the teacher's quality while being far cheaper to run on laptops and phones.

title: Fine-tuning versus prompting
text: Fine-tuning updates model weights on task-specific data, while prompting guides a frozen model with instructions and examples. For embedding models, fine-tuning on domain pairs can improve retrieval in specialized corpora.

title: Evaluating embedding quality
text: Embedding quality is commonly measured with Recall at K and nDCG on a labeled query set. Comparing metrics before and after quantization shows whether compressed weights still retrieve the right documents.

title: What is a vector database
text: A vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and supports nearest neighbor search. It keeps vectors together with document text and metadata so applications can retrieve original sources, not just identifiers.

title: Approximate nearest neighbor search
text: Exact nearest neighbor scan is too slow for millions of vectors, so vector indexes such as HNSW build graph structures that approximate the closest neighbors with high recall and low latency.

title: Cosine similarity for embeddings
text: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitude. Normalized embeddings make cosine similarity equivalent to a dot product, which is why many retrieval systems normalize vectors at write time.

title: Hybrid search explained
text: Hybrid search combines full-text keyword search with vector similarity search and fuses both ranked lists into one result. Reciprocal Rank Fusion is a popular method that rewards documents appearing high in either list.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion details
text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion scores each document by summing contributions of the form one over k plus rank from every result list. The constant k dampens the influence of top positions and stabilizes the fused ordering.

title: Full-text indexes and inverted files
text: A full-text index is an inverted file that maps each term to the documents containing it. Keyword search ranks candidates with scoring functions such as BM25 that reward term frequency and rarity.

title: Incremental ingestion and index refresh
text: When new documents are written to a search engine they may not be visible until the index refresh completes. Systems either expose an explicit flush call or make small writes searchable synchronously.

title: Metadata filtering in retrieval
text: Metadata filtering narrows retrieval to documents whose fields match conditions, for example category equals AI or year greater than 2023. Combining metadata filters with vector search keeps results both relevant and compliant.

title: WebGPU API overview
text: WebGPU is a modern graphics and compute API for the web that exposes the GPU through a low-level interface. Machine learning frameworks use WebGPU to run neural network inference directly in the browser.

title: WebAssembly execution model
text: WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs at near-native speed inside a sandbox. When a device has no usable GPU, ONNX Runtime Web falls back to a WebAssembly execution provider for CPU inference.

title: Running AI models in the browser
text: Libraries like Transformers.js load ONNX model files into the browser and execute them with ONNX Runtime Web. All computation happens on the user device, which preserves privacy and removes cloud inference costs.

title: WebGPU compute shaders for inference
text: WebGPU compute shaders allow general purpose parallel computation on the GPU. Embedding models run as a graph of dispatches, and half precision floats keep memory bandwidth low on consumer GPUs.

title: Browser storage and caching models
text: The browser Cache API and IndexedDB let web apps persist downloaded model weights across sessions. A second visit can load the model from local cache instead of re-downloading hundreds of megabytes.

title: Web workers for background inference
text: Web workers run scripts on background threads so heavy embedding computation does not freeze the user interface. Progress events from the worker keep the interface responsive during batch inference.

title: Content Security Policy for web apps
text: Content Security Policy headers restrict which scripts a page may load, protecting users from cross site scripting. Applications that fetch models from a CDN must allowlist the model host.

title: Progressive web app basics
text: A progressive web app installs on the device and works offline with service worker caching. Local-first applications such as personal knowledge bases benefit from this offline capability.

title: Information retrieval evaluation metrics
text: Recall at K measures how many relevant documents appear in the top K results, while nDCG rewards placing the most relevant documents at the top. Both metrics need a labeled query document set.

title: The BM25 scoring function
text: BM25 scores a document for a query using term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalization. It remains a strong keyword baseline even in the age of neural retrieval.

title: Query expansion techniques
text: Query expansion adds synonyms or related terms to the original query to improve recall. Vector retrieval achieves a similar effect automatically because nearby embeddings cover paraphrases.

title: Dense retrieval versus sparse retrieval
text: Sparse retrieval matches exact terms through inverted indexes, while dense retrieval matches semantic meaning through embeddings. Hybrid systems run both and fuse rankings to cover each other's weaknesses.

title: Chunking documents for retrieval
text: Long documents are split into chunks before embedding so each vector represents a focused passage. Chunk size and overlap directly affect retrieval granularity and the precision of returned evidence.

title: Reranking with cross encoders
text: A cross encoder reads a query and a candidate document together and outputs a relevance score. Rerankers are slower than bi-encoders but more accurate, so they usually refine only the top candidates.

title: Relational database fundamentals
text: Relational databases organize data into tables with typed columns and enforce integrity through keys and constraints. SQL remains the standard language for querying these tables.

title: SQL window functions
text: Window functions compute aggregates across a set of rows while keeping every row visible, which makes running totals and rankings straightforward without self joins.

title: Database indexes and query plans
text: An index speeds up lookups by keeping a sorted structure over a column, and the query planner chooses among available indexes using estimated costs. Reading the query plan reveals full table scans.

title: Transaction isolation levels
text: Isolation levels from read committed to serializable define how concurrently running transactions observe each other's changes. Stronger isolation trades throughput for fewer anomalies.

title: Distributed database consistency
text: Distributed databases replicate data across nodes and must balance consistency, availability and latency. Consensus protocols such as Paxos and Raft keep replicas agreeing on one committed history.

title: OceanBase distributed architecture
text: OceanBase is a distributed relational database that shards tables across zones and uses Paxos based replicas for high availability. It is MySQL and Oracle compatible for easy migration.

title: Embedded database engines
text: An embedded database runs inside the application process with no separate server, which simplifies local deployment. SQLite is the classic example, and vector capable embedded engines bring semantic search to local apps.

title: Data warehouse versus data lake
text: A data warehouse stores curated, schema-on-write tables for analytics, while a data lake keeps raw data in open formats until processing time. Many platforms now blend both in a lakehouse.

title: Node.js event loop concurrency
text: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single event loop thread and delegates blocking work to libuv thread pools. Async I/O keeps a server responsive while file and network operations complete in the background.

title: npm package management
text: npm installs dependencies declared in package.json and records resolved versions in the lockfile. Lockfiles make continuous integration builds reproducible across machines.

title: Express web server basics
text: Express is a minimal Node.js web framework where middleware functions process each request in order. It commonly serves static files plus a JSON REST API from one process.

title: REST API design practices
text: Good REST APIs use resource oriented paths, correct HTTP methods and meaningful status codes. Consistent error bodies help clients handle failures without parsing error strings.

title: Git branching workflows
text: Feature branches isolate changes until they are reviewed and merged, and rebase keeps the history linear. Continuous integration runs tests on every push to catch regressions early.

title: Docker containers for local development
text: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image, so the same container runs identically on every machine. Local development stacks often compose a database service next to the app.

title: Visual Studio Code extensions
text: VS Code extensions add language servers, linters and debuggers to the editor. The extension host runs each language server as a separate process for isolation.

title: Personal knowledge management tools
text: Personal knowledge tools collect notes, clippings and documents into a searchable library. Local semantic search lets users find notes by meaning instead of remembering exact keywords.

title: Building a personal RAG assistant
text: A retrieval augmented generation assistant indexes your own notes and documents, retrieves the most relevant passages for a question, and passes them to a language model. Doing retrieval locally keeps private files on the device.

title: Note taking with markdown files
text: Plain markdown files keep notes portable across editors and tools. A local indexer can embed each file and sync only changed files into the search index.
